- CMSAlgorithm now carries KMAC128_KDF and KMAC256_KDF, the NIST id-KMAC128 and id-KMAC256 identifiers (2.16.840.1.101.3.4.2.21 and .22) the KEM recipient KDF handling already accepted.

- The specifications document now carries a post-quantum transition section (4.1) summarising NIST IR 8547 for users of the library: which algorithms are standardised and which are still candidates, the recommended parameter sets and their security categories, the pre-hash digest rule, how the library supports hybrids in TLS, key agreement and signatures, the restriction of the stateful hash-based schemes to uses such as firmware signing, and the 2030 deprecation and 2035 disallow dates for the quantum-vulnerable algorithms (NIST), kept apart from the US federal key establishment and signature deadlines of Executive Order 14412. The KEM tables no longer describe ML-KEM as a finalist or HQC as a round 4 candidate, and the signers section now places the standardised post-quantum signatures under org.bouncycastle.crypto.

- The SP 800-232 Ascon algorithms are now in the BC provider: Cipher, KeyGenerator and AlgorithmParameters "ASCON-AEAD128" (128 bit key, 128 bit nonce generated when none is given, 128 bit tag) and MessageDigest "ASCON-HASH256", "ASCON-XOF128" and "ASCON-CXOF128" (the XOFs with a 256 bit output, CXOF with an empty customization string). They were previously light-weight only.

-- An uninitialised "ML-DSA" KeyPairGenerator now produces ML-DSA-65 keys rather than ML-DSA-87 ("HASH-ML-DSA" ML-DSA-65-WITH-SHA512), the category 3 set that matches the ML-KEM-768 default NIST recommends; and the ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA generators now draw from the provider's 256 bit DEFAULT DRBG wherever the caller gives no SecureRandom - when uninitialised, when obtained under a parameter set name such as "ML-DSA-44" and used without initialize(), and for SLH-DSA also on initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec) - rather than from a platform SecureRandom. The ML-DSA-44 parameters now note that the set is NIST category 2 only with a random bit generator of at least 192 bits of security (NIST IR 8547, Table 3), and the ML-DSA and SLH-DSA Signature services now document that initSign() without a SecureRandom signs deterministically while one with a SecureRandom gives the "hedged" form FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 prefer.

+- An uninitialised "ML-DSA" KeyPairGenerator now produces ML-DSA-65 keys rather than ML-DSA-87 ("HASH-ML-DSA" ML-DSA-65-WITH-SHA512), the category 3 set that matches the ML-KEM-768 default NIST recommends; and the ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA generators now draw from the provider's 256 bit DEFAULT DRBG wherever the caller gives no SecureRandom - when uninitialised, when obtained under a parameter set name such as "ML-DSA-44" and used without initialize(), and for SLH-DSA also on initialize(AlgorithmParameterSpec) - rather than from a platform SecureRandom, unless a default SecureRandom has been set on CryptoServicesRegistrar, which is then used as it is by the other key pair generators. A generator obtained under a parameter set name creates its DRBG on first use, so one initialised with the caller's own SecureRandom never builds one. The new CryptoServicesRegistrar.isSecureRandomSpecified() reports whether a default SecureRandom has been set through setSecureRandom() or setSecureRandomProvider(). The ML-DSA-44 parameters now note that the set is NIST category 2 only with a random bit generator of at least 192 bits of security (NIST IR 8547, Table 3), and the ML-DSA and SLH-DSA Signature services now document that initSign() without a SecureRandom signs deterministically while one with a SecureRandom gives the "hedged" form FIPS 204 and FIPS 205 prefer.

- The BC provider's RFC 8439 ChaCha20 cipher ("ChaCha20"/"ChaCha7539") can now be started at a given block: it accepts the new org.bouncycastle.jcajce.spec.BCChaCha20ParameterSpec, which carries the nonce and initial block counter on any Java version, and from Java 11 the JDK's javax.crypto.spec.ChaCha20ParameterSpec, so it can serve the record number protection of DTLS 1.3 and the header protection of QUIC, including the JDK's own QUIC implementation when BC is the preferred provider. The counter is unsigned, each doFinal returns to the initial block, and getParameters() returns null for a non-zero counter, as the JDK's ChaCha20 does, since AlgorithmParameters cannot carry it. Previously only an IvParameterSpec was accepted, so the key stream always started at block 0.
